title: Building a home gym in a cold environment
summary: Five considerations for a garage or shed gym in an arctic or poorly insulated location: experience a winter before building, don't trust insulation, don't count on heaters to fight outside cold, be honest about your cold tolerance, and expect frozen barbells and bands. His own gym sometimes dropped to 15-20 F with heat running.

claims.claim: Don't build a garage gym right after moving somewhere in spring or summer; live through a winter first to know how cold it gets.
He planned his gym about 8 months earlier, already knowing the local cold after living there a long time.
Walking into a cold gym after an 8-hour workday saps all your energy.
Don't trust insulation: unless the gym is inside the house, a garage or shed exposed to the elements will get cold, and a garage door lets in cold air even when sealed.
Where he lives, winter lasts about 8 months a year; his gym dropped as low as 15-20 F even with the heat running.
A furnace or heater in a garage gym only provides relief; it fights the outside cold and won't raise the temperature like in a house.
If you feel cold at 40-50 F, don't build a gym that exposes you to cold daily; you'll be miserable and your relationship with training will become toxic.
He tolerates cold extremely well (coat and T-shirt in snowstorms) and never skipped a session even during a polar vortex at -15 to -20 F outside.
His weakness is humidity; he can't train when it's humid and would not build a gym where he couldn't control it.
Cold tolerance depends on bodyfat and genetics; if you lack it, cold will hurt your gains, so don't just assume you'll get used to it.
Steel barbells freeze and numb your hands, which is painful and can be dangerous on lifts like bench where you need to feel the bar.
Resistance bands freeze at low enough temperatures and lose all elasticity, becoming useless.
